content: Dimethyl sulfide (DMS), also known as methylthiomethane, is an organic compound containing sulfur with the chemical formula (CH3)2S. In its concentrated liquid form, DMS is flammable, insoluble, and has a boiling point of 37°C. It emits a disagreeable odor. In vapor form, DMS is released during the cooking of certain vegetables, such as corn and cabbage, as well as seafood. It is also a marker of bacterial contamination in malt production and brewing processes. DMS is a degradation product of dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) and is also generated through bacterial metabolism of methanethiol. DMS is the most abundant biologically derived sulfur compound emitted into the atmosphere, primarily over oceans by phytoplankton. While Andrew Johnston of the University of East Anglia has described DMS as the smell of the sea, it is more accurate to state that DMS is one component of this characteristic odor, alongside algal pheromones known as dictyopterenes. DMS is also naturally produced through bacterial transformation of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) waste, which, when disposed of into sewers, can lead to environmental odor issues. In the marine atmosphere, DMS undergoes oxidation to form various sulfur-containing compounds, including sulfur dioxide, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), dimethyl sulfone, methanesulfonic acid, and sulfuric acid. Among these, sulfuric acid can contribute to the formation of new aerosols that act as cloud condensation nuclei. This interaction with cloud formation suggests that the large-scale production of atmospheric DMS over oceans may significantly influence Earth's climate. Recent studies indicate that marine bacteria may be reducing the release of this critical climate-cooling gas from the oceans. In industrial applications, DMS is utilized in petroleum refining and petrochemical production to control the formation of coke and carbon monoxide. It is also employed to mitigate dust in steel mills. DMS plays a role in various organic synthesis processes and is a byproduct of Swern oxidation. Additionally, it is used as a food flavoring agent. DMS can be oxidized, either naturally or artificially, to produce dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), which possesses valuable solvent properties. The largest global producer of DMS is Gaylord Chemical Corporation, which is a key economic contributor to the paper industry in Bogalusa, Louisiana. From a safety perspective, dimethyl sulfide is flammable and acts as an irritant. Even at extremely low concentrations, it has an unpleasant odor.
